paras: The lynching of Francisco Jimeno was the hanging of a young sheepherder by about one hundred citizens near Lompoc, at Santa Rita in Santa Barbara County, California, in early April 1881. Jimeno, described as Mexican or Indian, was held on suspicion of the rape and murder of Mrs. Louisa Sargent and was taken after the inquest and hanged to a tree near the scene. The local press applauded the hanging, while some eastern papers soon reported that the wrong man had been lynched.

According to a Lompoc special to the Santa Barbara Press, Mrs. Sargent of Santa Rita set out alone on horseback on Saturday, April 2, to visit a neighbor, and her husband later found her horse grazing by the road. The next morning the community turned out and found her body buried near a sheep camp, her head crushed as if by a club. She was about twenty, the wife of John H. Sargent and a daughter of E. C. Kelley. A sheepherder found near the spot was arrested, and dispatches of April 4 warned that he was in danger of being lynched.

Justice of the Peace A. Lansdell held an inquest on the body, at which Jimeno denied any knowledge of the crime and said he had been asleep under a tree. When the inquest ended, one hundred citizens took him and hung him to a limb for some seconds. Lowered, he said he had seen another man rape and kill Mrs. Sargent and that, fearing suspicion because the body lay near his cabin, he had dragged it about 400 yards with a rope and buried it in a gulch.

He then led the citizens to the buried club, her hat and the tin pail she had carried, and his shoes were said to fit the footprints. Because his stories about the other man conflicted and he would give no name, the crowd judged his guilt proven and strung him up to the limb of a tree near the spot. The body was left hanging until the following afternoon; a Santa Barbara dispatch dated April 5 placed the hanging on the previous night, while a Connecticut item said Tuesday, April 5.

Mrs. Sargent's funeral, conducted by the Rev. J. W. Webb, drew a very large crowd, and business houses closed. Parties went in search of Jimeno's brother, and on April 6 he was caught by what one report called the Santa Barbara vigilance committee, denied any part and offered an alibi, while the citizens promised a 'fair trial' and execution if he proved guilty. A Los Alamos special of April 9 said the brother proved his alibi through his employers and was released, but was so frightened by the vigilantes that he fled to the brush. No report of an inquest into Jimeno's death or of any arrest for the hanging appears in the coverage.

Western papers carried local specials to the Santa Barbara Press, and the Los Angeles Herald's version said county sentiment fully justified the hanging. The Gold Hill Daily News headed an editorial 'Justice' and quoted the Santa Barbara Press: 'All honor to Lompoc' and 'Away with the farce of jury trials.'

A San Francisco wire describing the brief first hanging ran in Chicago under 'LYNCHED.', in Wheeling as 'A Ravisher Hanged by Degrees in California', and as far as Pickens, South Carolina. Other eastern items took a different line: the Morning Journal and Courier headed its report 'An Innocent Man Lynched', and the Wheeling Register later printed 'The Wrong Man Lynched by a California Crowd', blaming 'a maddened mob of lynchers.' By mid-April the story had shrunk to a one-line brief in Kansas and Indiana weeklies naming him 'Francisco Timino.'

Accounts differ on who Jimeno was: early dispatches called him Mexican, later Santa Barbara and San Luis Obispo dispatches 'a full-blooded Indian', and the Lompoc special 'Indian or Mexican.' Wires of April 5 and 7 said Santa Barbara now believed his older brother was the murderer and that many citizens had protested the execution, but the April 9 report of the brother's proven alibi does not support that version.

reader.title: Lynching of Francisco Jimeno
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
bases: About one hundred citizens took the arrested sheepherder after the inquest and hanged him to a tree (A7, A8, A9).

Francisco Jimeno, held on suspicion of the rape and murder of Mrs. Louisa Sargent, was hanged without trial by a crowd of about one hundred citizens who judged his guilt proven (A7, A8, A9); the papers call it a lynching and the work of 'Vigilantes' (A6, A13). He was described as Mexican or Indian, not Black (A4, A7), so the case falls outside anti-Black violence.

A Lompoc special to the Santa Barbara Press (A7, A8), a San Luis Obispo dispatch (A9) and the San Francisco wire (A6) independently report the hanging by citizens after the inquest; they differ on his ethnicity, the timing and his guilt, not on the killing.

accounts.label: Lompoc special to the Santa Barbara Press
accounts.gist: After Justice Lansdell's inquest, one hundred citizens hung Jimeno to a limb for some seconds; lowered, he said he had seen another man commit the crime and had dragged and buried the body; he dug up the club, hat and pail, told conflicting stories and was strung up to a tree.

accounts.label: San Luis Obispo dispatch
accounts.gist: An Indian herder, after capture, said an unknown Mexican killed her and he buried her out of compassion; his shoes fitted the tracks and nearly 100 citizens hanged him near the spot and left him hanging.

accounts.label: San Francisco wire
accounts.gist: A sheep herder was hanged a few seconds by citizens after the inquest, made a statement, and was then hanged to a tree because his stories conflicted.

accounts.label: Later wires (innocence)
accounts.gist: Reports from April 5 and 7 said Santa Barbara people now believed his brother was the murderer, that many citizens had protested the execution, and that Francisco could not have committed the crime.

framing.detail: The Santa Barbara Press (quoted) wrote 'All honor to Lompoc' and 'Away with the farce of jury trials'; the Gold Hill Daily News headed its editorial 'Justice' and called the murderer an 'infernal fiend'.
The Los Angeles Herald's Lompoc special called him 'the murderer' and said public sentiment in the county fully justified the hanging.
The San Francisco wire ran under 'LYNCHED.' in Chicago and as 'LYNCHING MATINEE. A Ravisher Hanged by Degrees in California' in Wheeling, and without headline in Pickens, S.C.

The Morning Journal and Courier headed its item 'An Innocent Man Lynched' while reporting that public opinion justified the execution; the Wheeling Register later ran 'MISTAKEN MURDERERS. The Wrong Man Lynched by a California Crowd.'

conflicts.note: The first reports called him Mexican; the Gold Hill 'LATER' item corrected this to Indian.
